blocks.x: A letter can stand for a number you do not know yet, or for one that is free to change. That lets one short line of math cover a whole family of situations instead of a single fixed case. Numbers and letters stitched together with the usual operations form an expression, like \(3x + 5\). Nothing you already know gets thrown out, since a letter is just a stand-in for a number. Two conventions to keep for good. \(3x\) means \(3 \times x\), and \(x^2\) means \(x \times x\).

A bead bracelet holds \(3\) colored beads per charm plus \(4\) fixed clasp beads, so a bracelet with \(n\) charms has \(3n + 4\) beads. A customer orders \(6\) charms. Evaluate \(3n + 4\) at \(n = 6\) by replacing \(n\) with \(6\). How many beads are on that bracelet? Type the single number.
hints: The expression is \(3n + 4\). To evaluate at \(n = 6\), swap the letter \(n\) for the number \(6\) everywhere it appears. You should be looking at \(3(6) + 4\).
Do the multiplication first. \(3(6)\) means \(3 \times 6\), which is \(18\). Then add the \(4\) clasp beads.
blocks.sol: Replace \(n\) with \(6\) in \(3n + 4\). $$3(6) + 4 = 18 + 4 = 22.$$ The bracelet has \(\boxed{22}\) beads. Build the expression once and it handles any order, since a new charm count is just a new value to drop in.

blocks.x: A diver's height in meters is \(11 - 4t\), where \(t\) counts minutes of descent. An expression splits into terms separated by signs, here \(11\) and \(-4t\). The number multiplying \(t\), carried with its sign, is the coefficient of \(t\). Read off the coefficient of \(t\) and type that single value, sign included.
hints: A subtraction is really an addition of a negative. Rewrite \(11 - 4t\) as \(11 + (-4t)\) so the sign on the \(t\) term sits right out in the open.
The coefficient of \(t\) is the whole number multiplying \(t\), the minus included. In \(-4t\) that number is \(-4\).
blocks.sol: Read \(11 - 4t\) as \(11 + (-4t)\). The term built from \(t\) is \(-4t\), so the coefficient of \(t\) is \(\boxed{-4}\). The minus belongs to the coefficient, not to the term next door. The lone \(11\) is the constant term, the diver's starting height.

blocks.x: Different letters stand for different kinds, so \(x\) and \(y\) never combine. In \(3x + 5y + 2x + y\), gather the \(x\) terms with each other and the \(y\) terms with each other, remembering the lone \(y\) means \(1y\). After you simplify, what is the coefficient of \(x\)? Type that single value.
hints: Sort the terms into two piles before you add anything. One pile holds the \(x\) terms, the other holds the \(y\) terms. A term with \(x\) can never land in the \(y\) pile, so the two letters get counted separately.
Add the \(x\) terms by themselves, \(3x + 2x = 5x\), and leave the \(y\) terms alone. The number sitting in front of \(x\) is its coefficient, so read that off.
blocks.sol: Gather the \(x\) terms, \(3x + 2x = 5x\), and the \(y\) terms, remembering the lone \(y\) means \(1y\), so \(5y + y = 6y\). That gives $$3x + 5y + 2x + y = 5x + 6y.$$ The coefficient of \(x\) is \(\boxed{5}\). Different letters stand for different things, so an \(x\) term and a \(y\) term never combine.

blocks.cap: Only matching shapes combine. Four \(x\)-strips and one more make \(5x\). An \(x^2\) square is a different shape and \(y\) is a different letter, so neither joins the \(x\) pile.

blocks.x: Sort by shape before combining. In \(x^2 + 5x + 2x^2 + 3\), the squares belong with squares and the strips with strips. A thing squared and the thing itself are different kinds of object, so \(x^2\) and \(5x\) do not merge, which is exactly why counting terms is a real question. Write \(x^2 + 5x + 2x^2 + 3\) in simplest form. How many terms does it have once fully simplified? Type the single count.
hints: Sort the four pieces by their shape before you add anything. Which ones are square tiles \(x^2\), which is a strip \(5x\), and which is a plain number? Only pieces of the same shape can be combined.

Combine just the squares, \(x^2 + 2x^2 = 3x^2\), and leave \(5x\) and \(3\) exactly where they are since nothing matches them. That gives \(3x^2 + 5x + 3\). Now count the separate pieces joined by plus signs.
blocks.sol: Combine the squares, \(x^2 + 2x^2 = 3x^2\). The \(5x\) and the \(3\) have nothing matching them, so $$x^2 + 5x + 2x^2 + 3 = 3x^2 + 5x + 3.$$ The pieces are \(3x^2\), \(5x\), and \(3\), which is \(\boxed{3}\) terms. Squaring \(x\) makes a different kind of object than \(x\) itself, so those two never fold together.

blocks.x: Read an expression, then simplify it. To evaluate, replace every letter with its value and finish the arithmetic. Build the expression once, then evaluate it as often as you like. An expression splits into terms at its plus and minus signs, and the number in front of a term, sign included, is its coefficient, so a lone \(x\) means \(1x\) and \(-x\) means \(-1x\), while a plain number is a constant. Two terms are like terms only when their variable parts match exactly, and then you combine them just by adding coefficients, since \(x+x=2x\). If the variable parts differ at all, with \(x^2\) beside \(x\), or \(x\) beside \(y\), they are different kinds of thing and never merge, which is why the count of terms in simplest form actually means something.
Nobody used a letter for the unknown until the 1500s. Viète introduced vowels, and Descartes shifted to \(x, y, z\), possibly because his printer had plenty of spare \(x\) type blocks.

blocks.cap: Cutting the width into two pieces cuts the area into two pieces, so a rectangle of height \(a\) and width \(b+c\) has the same area as the two slabs \(ab\) and \(ac\) put together. Multiplying a group hands the multiplier to every piece inside, which is why \(7(y+2)\) becomes \(7y+14\), as plainly as cutting the rectangle down the middle.

blocks.x: A school orders supply kits in two batches, \(3(x+5) + 4(x+8)\), where each kit holds \(x\) notebooks plus some pens. Distribute each group on its own, then combine the like terms so the order collapses to (notebooks)\(\,x\,\) plus (pens). How many pens does the order come to? Type that single number.
hints: Open each group separately. The first group \(3(x+5)\) becomes \(3x + 15\), and the second group \(4(x+8)\) becomes \(4x + 32\). The pens are the plain numbers with no \(x\) attached.
Add the two plain-number pieces together. You have \(15\) pens from the first batch and \(32\) pens from the second, so the total number of pens is \(15 + 32\).
blocks.sol: Distribute each group. \(3(x+5) = 3x + 15\) and \(4(x+8) = 4x + 32\), so the order reads \(3x + 15 + 4x + 32\). Combine like terms, \(3x + 4x = 7x\) and \(15 + 32 = 47\), which gives $$7x + 47.$$ The pens are the plain number with no \(x\) on it, so the order comes to \(\boxed{47}\) pens.

blocks.x: This one leans on signs, so go slowly. Expand \(5(z - 3) + 3(7 - 2z)\), letting each subtraction ride along with its term and remembering \(3 \times (-2z) = -6z\). Combine the like terms all the way to one cleanest form, then read off the coefficient of \(z\). Type that single value, sign included.
hints: Line up your four pieces, \(5z - 15 + 21 - 6z\), then sort them into z terms and plain numbers. The coefficient of \(z\) is whatever number ends up sitting in front of \(z\) once you have gathered \(5z\) and \(-6z\) together.
Add the z terms by adding their coefficients, \(5 + (-6) = -1\), so the z part becomes \(-z\). Writing \(-z\) is the same as writing \(-1z\), so the coefficient is that \(-1\).
blocks.sol: Distribute both groups, letting the subtractions travel with their terms. \(5(z - 3) = 5z - 15\), and \(3(7 - 2z) = 21 - 6z\) since \(3 \times (-2z) = -6z\). That gives \(5z - 15 + 21 - 6z\). The z terms combine as \(5z - 6z = -z\), and the constants as \(-15 + 21 = 6\), so the simplest form is \(-z + 6\). Since \(-z\) means \(-1z\), the coefficient of \(z\) is \(\boxed{-1}\).

blocks.x: A subtraction in front of a group flips the sign of everything inside, since the multiplier carries its minus into every piece. Take \(8 - 2(x - 5)\). The \(-2\) lands on both the \(x\) and the \(-5\), so the \(-5\) becomes \(+10\), not \(-10\). Distribute, combine the constants, and the expression collapses to (something)\(\,x\,\) plus a constant. What is the constant term once fully simplified? Type that single value.
hints: The number multiplying the group is the whole \(-2\), not just \(2\). Send it onto both pieces inside, so \(-2 \times x\) and \(-2 \times (-5)\). Watch what happens to that second sign.
A negative times a negative is positive, so \(-2 \times (-5) = +10\). That gives \(8 - 2x + 10\). Add the two loose numbers \(8 + 10\) to get the constant, and read it off.
blocks.sol: The \(-2\) multiplies both pieces inside, so \(-2 \times x = -2x\) and \(-2 \times (-5) = +10\). $$8 - 2(x - 5) = 8 - 2x + 10 = -2x + 18.$$ The constant term is \(\boxed{18}\). The usual slip is sending only the \(2\) inside and landing on \(-10\), but the minus rides along with it.

blocks.x: Distribute to every piece. When a number sits in front of a group, hand it to every piece inside, not just the first, so \(3(x+4)=3x+12\) with the \(3\) reaching all the way to the back. A minus in front of a group is really multiplying by \(-1\), so it flips the sign of every piece inside, and \(-(x-5)=-x+5\). Almost every distribution slip is a term the multiplier never reached.

Two expressions are equivalent when they agree for every value of the variable. Staring at them is not proof, so use this grading check. Build the difference \(A - B\) and plug in a value. If they truly are equivalent, that difference must come out \(0\). Let \(A = 2(3x+4) + x\) and \(B = 7x + 8\). Compute \(A - B\) at \(x = 5\) and type the single number you get.
hints: Evaluating at \(x = 5\) means replacing every \(x\) with \(5\). Find the value of \(A = 2(3x + 4) + x\) at \(x = 5\), then the value of \(B = 7x + 8\) at \(x = 5\), and finally subtract the second from the first.
blocks.sol: At \(x = 5\), \(A = 2(3 \cdot 5 + 4) + 5 = 2 \cdot 19 + 5 = 43\) and \(B = 7 \cdot 5 + 8 = 43\), so \(A - B = 43 - 43 = \boxed{0}\). Simplifying \(A\) shows this was never luck. \(2(3x + 4) + x = 6x + 8 + x = 7x + 8\), which is exactly \(B\), so the difference is \(0\) at every value of \(x\).

blocks.x: The target is \(6n + 10\), and four suspects line up beside it: \(2(3n+5)\), \(3(2n+4)\), \(5 + 6n + 5\), and \(10 + 6n\). Simplify each one until you can compare it cleanly with \(6n + 10\). How many of the four are equivalent to \(6n + 10\)? Type the single count.
hints: To test a suspect, rewrite it in the same plain form as the target, which is some number of \(n\) plus a constant. For the ones with parentheses, multiply the outside number by each piece inside. For the ones that are already a string of terms, gather the loose numbers together.

Suspect one becomes \(6n + 10\), a match. Suspect two becomes \(6n + 12\), so its constant is off by 2 and it fails. Suspect three has \(5 + 5 = 10\) so it is \(6n + 10\), a match. Suspect four is \(10 + 6n\), the same two pieces just written in the other order, which is still a match. Now count the matches.
blocks.sol: Rewrite each suspect and line it up against \(6n + 10\). \(2(3n + 5) = 6n + 10\), a match. \(3(2n + 4) = 6n + 12\), and \(12 \ne 10\), so it fails. \(5 + 6n + 5 = 6n + 10\), a match. \(10 + 6n\) is the same two pieces in the other order, a match. That is \(\boxed{3}\) of the four. Reordering a sum never changes its value, so writing the constant first does not make a new expression.

blocks.x: Equivalence. Two expressions are equivalent when they agree for every value of the variable. Testing values is lopsided. If two expressions disagree even once, you are done, they cannot be equivalent, but matching at one lucky value, or even a few, proves nothing. The only sure way is to rewrite both to the same simplest form. Reordering a sum keeps its meaning, so \(x+7\) and \(7+x\) are the same, but \(x-7\) and \(7-x\) are not, because subtraction is not symmetric.

Coefficients do not have to be whole numbers. A fraction can sit in front of a variable, and combining such terms is the same common-denominator move from Chapter 4 with an \(x\) riding along. The terms \(\tfrac{2x}{3}\) and \(\tfrac{5x}{7}\) are like terms, since both carry a single \(x\). Combine \(\tfrac{2x}{3} + \tfrac{5x}{7}\) into one term, then state the coefficient of \(x\) as a fraction in lowest terms, typed as a over b.
hints: Both terms are like terms, so think of this as adding the coefficients \(\tfrac{2}{3}\) and \(\tfrac{5}{7}\) while the \(x\) just rides along. To add those fractions you need a common denominator for \(3\) and \(7\).

A common denominator of \(3\) and \(7\) is \(21\). Rewrite \(\tfrac{2x}{3}\) as \(\tfrac{14x}{21}\) and \(\tfrac{5x}{7}\) as \(\tfrac{15x}{21}\), then add the numerators over \(21\). The coefficient of \(x\) is whatever fraction lands in front.
blocks.sol: A common denominator of \(3\) and \(7\) is \(21\). Rewrite each term with denominator \(21\), so \(\tfrac{2x}{3} = \tfrac{14x}{21}\) and \(\tfrac{5x}{7} = \tfrac{15x}{21}\). Now add the numerators over the shared denominator. $$\frac{2x}{3} + \frac{5x}{7} = \frac{14x}{21} + \frac{15x}{21} = \frac{29x}{21}$$ That single term is \(\tfrac{29x}{21}\), and its coefficient of \(x\) is \(\tfrac{29}{21}\). Since \(29\) is prime and does not divide \(21\), the fraction is already in lowest terms. The coefficient of \(x\) is \(\boxed{29/21}\).

blocks.x: Fractional coefficients. A fraction in front of a letter never starts a new kind of math, since \(\tfrac{2x}{3}\) is just \(\tfrac{2}{3}\) of an \(x\). Adding two such terms is the same common-denominator work you already know, with the \(x\) left untouched. Find the shared bottom, rebuild each coefficient over it, add the numerators, and write the \(x\) back beside the answer. Every fraction skill you already have still applies here.

Sometimes the pieces you are adding live over different denominators, and one piece can be an expression. Combine \(\tfrac{a}{2} + \tfrac{6a - 5}{4}\) onto a common bottom, then write the result as a coefficient of \(a\) plus a constant, like \(2a - \tfrac{5}{4}\). In that clean form, type the constant term as a fraction in lowest terms, with its sign.
hints: The two denominators are \(2\) and \(4\), and \(4\) is a multiple of \(2\), so \(4\) is the common bottom. Rewrite \(\tfrac{a}{2}\) over \(4\) by doubling top and bottom, and leave \(\tfrac{6a-5}{4}\) exactly as it is. Then add the numerators over that one shared \(4\).

You have \(\tfrac{2a}{4} + \tfrac{6a-5}{4} = \tfrac{2a + 6a - 5}{4} = \tfrac{8a-5}{4}\). Split that into two fractions, \(\tfrac{8a}{4} - \tfrac{5}{4} = 2a - \tfrac{5}{4}\). The constant term is the piece with no \(a\) attached.
blocks.sol: The common denominator is \(4\), since \(4\) is a multiple of \(2\). Double the top and bottom of the first piece, leave the second alone, and add over the shared bottom. $$\tfrac{a}{2} + \tfrac{6a - 5}{4} = \tfrac{2a}{4} + \tfrac{6a - 5}{4} = \tfrac{2a + 6a - 5}{4} = \tfrac{8a - 5}{4}$$ Split that back into an \(a\) piece and a number piece, \(\tfrac{8a}{4} - \tfrac{5}{4} = 2a - \tfrac{5}{4}\). The constant term is \(\boxed{-5/4}\). The minus stays with the constant because the \(5\) was being subtracted inside the numerator.

blocks.x: This one expression gathers the whole lesson, a piece scaled by a fraction, a piece scaled by a whole number, and a piece over a denominator. Simplify \(\frac{1}{2}(4x + 6) + 3(x - 1) + \frac{x - 5}{3}\) all the way down to the form (something)\(\,x\,\) plus (something), then report the coefficient of \(x\) as a fraction in lowest terms, typed as a over b.
hints: Knock out one group at a time before you mix anything. Half of \(4x + 6\) gives \(2x + 3\). Three times \(x - 1\) gives \(3x - 3\), and watch that the \(3\) hits the \(-1\) too. The last group \(\frac{x - 5}{3}\) is one quantity divided by \(3\), so it splits into \(\frac{x}{3} - \frac{5}{3}\).

Now sweep up only the \(x\) terms and ignore the constants for this question. You have \(2x\), \(3x\), and \(\frac{x}{3}\), so the coefficient of \(x\) is \(2 + 3 + \frac{1}{3}\). Put \(2 + 3 = 5\) over a denominator of \(3\) to add the last piece, which makes \(\frac{15}{3} + \frac{1}{3}\).
blocks.sol: Take the three groups one at a time. \(\frac{1}{2}(4x + 6) = 2x + 3\), then \(3(x - 1) = 3x - 3\), then \(\frac{x - 5}{3} = \frac{x}{3} - \frac{5}{3}\). Lining them up gives \(2x + 3 + 3x - 3 + \frac{x}{3} - \frac{5}{3}\). The \(x\) coefficients add as \(2 + 3 + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{15}{3} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{16}{3}\), and the constants give \(3 - 3 - \frac{5}{3} = -\frac{5}{3}\), so the expression is \(\frac{16}{3}x - \frac{5}{3}\) and the coefficient of \(x\) is \(\boxed{16/3}\). It is already in lowest terms, since \(16\) and \(3\) share no factor.

review.x: A weather balloon's altitude in meters is \(13 - 7p\), where \(p\) is the number of minutes a valve has been venting. The number multiplying a variable, carried with its sign, is its coefficient. State the coefficient of \(p\) and type that single value, sign included.
hints: The expression \(13 - 7p\) has two pieces, a plain number \(13\) and a term built from \(p\). The coefficient lives in the term that contains \(p\).
The minus sign in front of \(7p\) belongs to the coefficient. So the term is \(-7p\), and the number multiplying \(p\) is not just \(7\).
review.sol: Reading the subtraction as adding a negative, \(13 - 7p\) is \(13 + (-7p)\). The term built from \(p\) is \(-7p\), so the coefficient of \(p\) is \(\boxed{-7}\). The minus belongs to the coefficient. The other term, \(13\), is the constant.

review.x: A print run is modeled by \(19 - 5q\), where \(q\) counts paper jams. The piece \(5q\) shifts as jams shift, but one piece does not change at all. That unchanging number is the constant term. State the constant term of \(19 - 5q\) and type that single number.
hints: The expression \(19 - 5q\) has two pieces. One piece has the letter \(q\) attached to it, and one piece is just a plain number with no letter.
The constant term is the part that stays the same no matter what \(q\) is. The \(5q\) piece depends on \(q\), so the constant term has to be the other piece.
review.sol: The two terms of \(19 - 5q\) are \(5q\), whose value shifts whenever \(q\) shifts, and \(19\), a plain number with no variable attached. The constant term is the one with no variable, so it is \(\boxed{19}\). Setting \(q = 0\) makes it visible, since \(19 - 5(0) = 19\).

review.x: A lone variable carries a hidden \(1\) in front, so \(m\) means \(1m\). Combine the like terms in \(3m + m + 5m\) into a single term, then type the coefficient of \(m\).
hints: Rewrite the lone \(m\) as \(1m\) so every term shows its number out front, giving \(3m + 1m + 5m\).
Add only the numbers in front, since they all count copies of the same \(m\). The coefficient is what sits in front of \(m\) once you finish.
review.sol: Every term here is a number of copies of \(m\), so they are like terms and can be merged. Reading the lone \(m\) as \(1m\), the expression becomes \(3m + 1m + 5m\). Add the numbers in front, \(3 + 1 + 5 = 9\), and keep the \(m\). The simplified expression is \(9m\). The coefficient of \(m\) is \(\boxed{9}\).

review.x: Tally each kind of term on its own, the plain numbers in one pile and the \(x\) terms in another. Simplify \(8 + 2x + 5 + 4x\), then read off the constant term and type that single value.
hints: Sort the four pieces into two groups. The plain numbers \(8\) and \(5\) belong together, and the \(x\) terms \(2x\) and \(4x\) belong together. You can add inside each group on its own.
Add the plain numbers to get the constant part, and add the \(x\) terms to get the \(x\) part. The constant term is the piece that has no \(x\) attached to it.
review.sol: Group the like terms first. The plain numbers are \(8\) and \(5\), and the \(x\) terms are \(2x\) and \(4x\). Combine each group on its own. The numbers give \(8 + 5 = 13\), and the \(x\) terms give \(2x + 4x = 6x\). Putting both groups back together, the expression in simplest form is \(6x + 13\). The constant term is the piece with no \(x\) attached to it, which is \(13\). So the value you type is \(\boxed{13}\).

review.x: Square tiles each cover \(x^2\) and thin tiles each cover \(x\), and the two kinds never combine because \(x^2\) and \(x\) are different objects. Gather each kind in \(5x^2 + 2x + 3x^2 + x\), write it in simplest form, then count how many terms remain.
hints: Sort the pieces into two piles. Put all the square \(x^2\) tiles together and all the thin \(x\) tiles together, then add up each pile on its own.
The \(x^2\) pile gives \(5x^2 + 3x^2 = 8x^2\) and the \(x\) pile gives \(2x + x = 3x\). Once you write those two results side by side, count the separate pieces joined by plus signs.
review.sol: Keep the two kinds of tiles separate while you combine. The square tiles give \(5x^2 + 3x^2 = 8x^2\), and the thin x-tiles give \(2x + x = 3x\). Putting the piles back together, the simplest form is \(8x^2 + 3x\). A term is one chunk separated by a plus or minus sign, so \(8x^2\) is one term and \(3x\) is another. They cannot merge into a single piece because a square tile is not the same kind of tile as a thin one. That leaves two terms. \(\boxed{2}\)

review.x: Since \(a\) and \(b\) stand for different things, an \(a\) term and a \(b\) term can never merge. Combine only the matching kinds in \(6a + 2b + a + 3b\), write the result in simplest form, then type how many terms are left.
hints: Group the like terms by sweeping up all the \(a\) pieces in one bundle and all the \(b\) pieces in another. You have \(6a\) and \(a\), and separately \(2b\) and \(3b\).
Adding the \(a\) pieces gives \(7a\), and adding the \(b\) pieces gives \(5b\). These cannot merge any further, so write the answer as a sum of those two bundles and then count the bundles.
review.sol: Collect the pieces of the same kind. The \(a\) terms give \(6a + a = 7a\), and the \(b\) terms give \(2b + 3b = 5b\), so $$6a + 2b + a + 3b = 7a + 5b.$$ That is two separate pieces joined by addition, so the count is \(\boxed{2}\). An \(a\) bundle and a \(b\) bundle measure different things, so they never merge into one term.

review.x: Expand \(8(3x + 2)\) by handing the \(8\) to every piece inside, so it lands on both the \(3x\) and the \(2\). In the result, the number multiplying \(x\) is its coefficient. What is the coefficient of \(x\)? Type that single value.
hints: Hand the \(8\) to each piece on its own. You get \(8 \times 3x\) for the first piece and \(8 \times 2\) for the second piece. Work those out and add them.
After expanding you have one term with an \(x\) and one plain number. The coefficient of \(x\) is just the number stuck to the \(x\), not the plain number at the end.
review.sol: Hand the \(8\) to every piece inside the group. \(8 \times 3x = 24x\) and \(8 \times 2 = 16\). Putting those together, the expanded expression is \(24x + 16\). No parentheses are left, so it is in simplest form. The term holding the \(x\) is \(24x\), and the number multiplying \(x\) is \(24\). That number is the coefficient of \(x\). So the coefficient is \(\boxed{24}\).

review.x: Distribute across each group in \(2(x+6) + 5(x+1)\), then combine the like terms into simplest form. Read off the constant term, the lone number with no \(x\) attached, and type that single value.
hints: Distribute first. \(2(x+6)\) becomes \(2x + 12\), and \(5(x+1)\) becomes \(5x + 5\). Now you have \(2x + 12 + 5x + 5\).
Group the \(x\) terms together and group the plain numbers together. The plain numbers are \(12\) and \(5\). The constant term is whatever they add up to.
review.sol: Distribute each group on its own. The first group gives \(2(x+6) = 2x + 12\), and the second gives \(5(x+1) = 5x + 5\). Putting those together, the expression is \(2x + 12 + 5x + 5\). Now combine like terms. The \(x\) terms are \(2x\) and \(5x\), which add to \(7x\). The plain numbers are \(12\) and \(5\), which add to \(17\). So in simplest form the expression is \(7x + 17\). The constant term is the number standing alone with no \(x\), which is \(17\). So the answer is \(\boxed{17}\).

review.x: Distribute each number across its own parentheses in \(6(n-2) + 4(5-3n)\), letting every sign ride along, then collect the like terms. In simplest form, read off the coefficient of \(n\) and type that single value, sign included.
hints: Distribute one chunk at a time. \(6(n - 2)\) becomes \(6n - 12\), and \(4(5 - 3n)\) becomes \(20 - 12n\). Notice the \(-3n\) keeps its minus sign when the \(4\) rides through.
Now gather the \(n\) terms together and the plain numbers together. The \(n\) terms are \(6n\) and \(-12n\). Combine them and the result is the coefficient you want.
review.sol: Distribute each factor across its parentheses, keeping every sign attached to its term. The first chunk gives \(6(n - 2) = 6n - 12\). The second chunk gives \(4(5 - 3n) = 20 - 12n\), where the \(4\) multiplies both the \(5\) and the \(-3n\). So far the expression reads \(6n - 12 + 20 - 12n\). Now collect like terms. The \(n\) terms are \(6n\) and \(-12n\), which combine to \(-6n\). The plain numbers are \(-12\) and \(20\), which combine to \(8\). The simplest form is \(-6n + 8\). The coefficient of \(n\) is the number multiplying \(n\), which is \(-6\). \(\boxed{-6}\)

review.x: In \(20 - 3(2x - 4)\), the \(-3\) distributes across the group and flips the sign of every piece inside because it is negative. Simplify into a number plus a multiple of \(x\), then find the constant term, the plain number with no \(x\), and type that single value.
hints: Distribute the \(-3\) across both terms inside the group. Watch the signs carefully. You get \(-3 \times 2x = -6x\) and \(-3 \times (-4) = +12\), since a negative times a negative is positive.
After distributing you have \(20 - 6x + 12\). The only like terms are the two plain numbers \(20\) and \(12\). Combine just those, and whatever number is left standing alone is the constant term.
review.sol: Distribute the \(-3\) into \(2x - 4\). You get \(-3 \times 2x = -6x\) and \(-3 \times (-4) = +12\), so the expression becomes \(20 - 6x + 12\). The plain numbers combine, \(20 + 12 = 32\), while \(-6x\) has no partner, leaving \(32 - 6x\). The constant term is \(\boxed{32}\). A negative multiplier flips the sign of every piece inside, which is where most slips happen.

review.x: Two expressions are equivalent when their difference \(A - B\) is \(0\) for every value of \(x\). Let \(A = 3(2x + 5)\) and \(B = 6x + 15\). Evaluate \(A - B\) at \(x = 4\) by replacing every \(x\) with \(4\), and type the single number you get.
hints: First open up \(A\). The \(3\) outside multiplies both pieces inside, so \(3(2x + 5)\) becomes \(6x + 15\). Now compare that to \(B = 6x + 15\).
Subtract carefully. \(A - B = (6x + 15) - (6x + 15)\). Line up the \(6x\) with the \(6x\) and the \(15\) with the \(15\), then see what is left before you even reach for \(x = 4\).
review.sol: At \(x = 4\), \(A = 3(2 \cdot 4 + 5) = 3 \cdot 13 = 39\) and \(B = 6 \cdot 4 + 15 = 39\), so \(A - B = 39 - 39 = \boxed{0}\). Distributing shows it could not have come out any other way, since \(3(2x + 5) = 6x + 15\) is exactly \(B\), so the difference is \(0\) for every value of \(x\).

review.x: The target is \(8x + 12\). Simplify each of \(4(2x + 3)\), \(2(4x + 6)\), \(8x + 6\), and \(12 + 8x\), then compare with the target. How many of the four are equivalent to \(8x + 12\)? Type the single count.
hints: Two expressions are equivalent when they give the same value for every choice of \(x\). To check, simplify each one by distributing any number sitting outside a set of parentheses, then line it up against \(8x + 12\).

Distributing means multiplying the outside number by each term inside, so \(4(2x + 3)\) becomes \(8x + 12\). Watch the third one carefully, the constant is \(6\) and not \(12\), and remember that \(12 + 8x\) is the same as \(8x + 12\) with the parts just written in the other order.
review.sol: Simplify each expression and compare it to the target \(8x + 12\). For the first, \(4(2x + 3) = 8x + 12\), which matches. For the second, \(2(4x + 6) = 8x + 12\), which also matches. For the third, \(8x + 6\) is already simplified, and its constant is \(6\) instead of \(12\), so it does not match. For the fourth, \(12 + 8x\) is the same two terms as \(8x + 12\) written in the other order, and order does not change the value, so it matches. Three of the four are equivalent to the target. \(\boxed{3}\)

review.x: Two dials add \(\tfrac{5x}{6}\) and \(\tfrac{x}{4}\) to a score, where \(x\) is the number of presses. Combine \(\tfrac{5x}{6} + \tfrac{x}{4}\) into one term using a common denominator of \(12\), keeping the \(x\). State the coefficient of \(x\) as a fraction in lowest terms, typed as a over b.
hints: A common denominator of \(12\) turns \(\tfrac{5x}{6}\) into \(\tfrac{10x}{12}\) and \(\tfrac{x}{4}\) into \(\tfrac{3x}{12}\). Now the two terms are ready to add.
Add the numerators over the shared \(12\) to get \(\tfrac{13x}{12}\). The coefficient of \(x\) is the fraction multiplying it, so it is \(\tfrac{13}{12}\), already in lowest terms.
review.sol: Rewrite each fraction with denominator \(12\). Since \(\tfrac{5x}{6} = \tfrac{10x}{12}\) and \(\tfrac{x}{4} = \tfrac{3x}{12}\), the sum becomes $$\frac{10x}{12} + \frac{3x}{12} = \frac{13x}{12}.$$ The combined term is \(\tfrac{13x}{12}\). The coefficient of \(x\) is the number multiplying it, which is \(\tfrac{13}{12}\). Since \(13\) is prime and does not divide \(12\), this fraction is already in lowest terms. The coefficient is \(\boxed{13/12}\).

review.x: A tiled border uses \(3(2s + 3)\) tiles in one row, \(2(s - 1)\) in another, plus \(5\) corner tiles, where \(s\) is a size setting. Build one expression for the total, simplify it, then evaluate at \(s = 4\) by replacing every \(s\) with \(4\). Type the single number you get.
hints: First expand each piece. \(3(2s + 3)\) becomes \(6s + 9\), and \(2(s - 1)\) becomes \(2s - 2\). Now add all the tiles together, including the \(5\) corner tiles.
Collect the \(s\) terms and the plain numbers separately. The \(s\) terms are \(6s + 2s = 8s\), and the numbers are \(9 - 2 + 5 = 12\), so the total is \(8s + 12\). Put \(s = 4\) into that.
review.sol: Start by expanding each grouped piece. The first row is \(3(2s + 3) = 6s + 9\), and the second row is \(2(s - 1) = 2s - 2\). Adding everything, including the \(5\) corner tiles, gives \(6s + 9 + 2s - 2 + 5\). Combine the like terms. The \(s\) terms give \(6s + 2s = 8s\), and the plain numbers give \(9 - 2 + 5 = 12\), so the simplified total is \(8s + 12\). Now evaluate at \(s = 4\) by replacing \(s\) with \(4\), which gives \(8 \cdot 4 + 12 = 32 + 12 = 44\). \(\boxed{44}\)

blocks.x: An expression like \(3x + 5\) just describes a whole family of values, one for each \(x\). Put an equals sign between two expressions, like \(3x + 5 = 20\), and you make a claim that both sides come out to the same number. That claim is an equation, and the value of the variable that makes it true is a solution. Two pictures help through this lesson. The equals sign is the level beam of a two-pan balance, and the variable is wrapped in layers of operations that you take off one at a time.

A vending machine charges \(3\) tokens to wake up plus \(5\) tokens per snack, so \(w\) snacks cost \(5w + 3\). One kid spent exactly \(23\) tokens, giving \(5w + 3 = 23\). With no method yet, test whole numbers. At \(w = 3\) the left side is \(18\), at \(w = 5\) it is \(28\), so the answer sits between. The value that makes both sides equal is the solution. What whole number \(w\) makes \(5w + 3 = 23\)? Type that value.
hints: You already passed \(23\) between \(w=3\) (which gives \(18\)) and \(w=5\) (which gives \(28\)). The answer is the whole number sitting right between them, so test the one you skipped.
Try \(w=4\). Then \(5w\) is \(5\times 4=20\), and \(20+3=23\). That hits the target exactly, so that is your solution.
blocks.sol: Try \(w=4\). Then \(5\times 4=20\), and \(20+3=23\), which is exactly the right side, so \(w=\boxed{4}\). Testing values works here because the left side climbs by \(5\) each step, so once \(23\) is bracketed between \(w=3\) and \(w=5\) only one whole number is left to check.

blocks.x: Before solving an equation you should be able to check one. Substituting means replacing every \(x\) with a candidate and seeing whether both sides match. A note claims \(x = 7\) solves \(3x - 5 = 19\), but \(3(7) - 5 = 16 \neq 19\), so \(7\) fails. One of the values \(7\) or \(8\) actually solves \(3x - 5 = 19\). Type the value that works.
hints: A correct solution must make the left side, \(3x - 5\), come out to exactly \(19\). You already saw \(7\) gives \(16\), which is too small, so test the other candidate.
Substitute \(x = 8\). The left side becomes \(3(8) - 5\). Work out \(3 \times 8 = 24\), then \(24 - 5\), and see whether you land on \(19\).
blocks.sol: Substitute \(x=8\). The left side is \(3(8)-5=24-5=19\), which matches the right side, so the value that works is \(\boxed{8}\). The other candidate fails, since \(3(7)-5=16\). Checking a value is always this direct, work out each side on its own and see whether they land on the same number.

blocks.x: Solution and checking. An equals sign claims the two sides are the same number, and a solution is the value of the variable that makes that claim true. The identities from 6.1 held for every value, but an equation like \(2x + 5 = 11\) is true for only one value of \(x\). Never take an answer on faith. Put it back into the original equation, work out each side on its own, and compare. If both sides land on the same number, your answer is a solution and the solving worked. If they do not, you have caught a slip, almost always a dropped negative sign.
The equals sign was invented by Robert Recorde in 1557. He chose two parallel lines because nothing could be more equal. The symbol took about a century to become standard.

A thermos starts at \(t\) degrees, the afternoon adds \(17\), and the display settles at \(9\), so \(t + 17 = 9\). The variable \(t\) is sealed inside an add-\(17\) box. Lift those \(17\) off the left pan, and lift the same \(17\) off the right pan to keep the scale level. Solve \(t + 17 = 9\) and type the value of \(t\).
hints: The \(17\) is added to \(t\). To undo an addition and free the variable, do the opposite operation to both sides at once. What single move strips that \(+17\) off the left pan?
Subtract \(17\) from both sides. The left pan becomes just \(t\), and the right pan becomes \(9 - 17\). That difference dips below zero, which is fine since the thermos started cold.
blocks.sol: Subtract \(17\) from both sides. $$t + 17 = 9$$ $$t + 17 - 17 = 9 - 17$$ $$t = \boxed{-8}$$ Checking, \(-8 + 17 = 9\), which matches the right side. A negative answer is fine here, it just means the thermos started below zero.

blocks.x: Six identical sandbags, each of unknown mass \(m\), together tip a balance to \(15\) units, so \(6m = 15\). The only thing wrapped around \(m\) is a times-\(6\), and division undoes multiplication, so divide both sides by \(6\) to leave one bag alone. The answer need not be a whole number, which is fine. Solve \(6m = 15\) and type \(m\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The variable is multiplied by \(6\), so to peel that away you do the opposite of multiplying. Divide both sides of the equation by \(6\).
Dividing both sides by \(6\) gives \(m = \frac{15}{6}\). Now reduce that fraction. Both \(15\) and \(6\) share a factor of \(3\), so cancel it to reach lowest terms.
blocks.sol: Divide both sides by \(6\). $$\frac{6m}{6} = \frac{15}{6}$$ The left side leaves \(m\) alone. On the right, \(15\) and \(6\) are both divisible by \(3\), so \(\frac{15}{6}\) reduces and each sandbag has mass $$\boxed{5/2}$$ Checking, \(6 \cdot \frac{5}{2} = \frac{30}{2} = 15\). A solution does not have to be a whole number.

blocks.x: The balance rule. Do the exact same thing to both sides and the beam stays level, so a value that made the equation true is still true afterward. Adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing both sides by the same nonzero amount rewrites the equation without changing its answer. The one forbidden move is changing one side and leaving the other alone, since that tips the scale and makes the equation false. Every solving step in this lesson is that one rule applied again and again.

blocks.cap: Removing the same weight from both pans keeps the scale level, which is why subtracting \(3\) from both sides of \(x+3=8\) leaves \(x=5\). The \(x\) never moved.

blocks.x: In \(4x - 9 = 7\), the variable sits inside two boxes, since it was multiplied by \(4\) first, then had \(9\) taken away. To unwrap, peel in reverse and pull the outer box off first, so add \(9\) to both sides, then divide by \(4\). Solve \(4x - 9 = 7\) and type the value of \(x\).
hints: The outer layer is the minus \(9\), so deal with it first. What can you add to both sides to undo subtracting \(9\)?
Add \(9\) to both sides to get \(4x = 16\). Now the variable sits in only the times-\(4\) box, so divide both sides by \(4\).
blocks.sol: Add \(9\) to both sides. $$4x - 9 + 9 = 7 + 9$$ That gives \(4x = 16\), so divide both sides by \(4\). $$\frac{4x}{4} = \frac{16}{4}$$ $$x = \boxed{4}$$ The \(-9\) came off first because it was the last thing done to \(x\). Checking, \(4(4) - 9 = 16 - 9 = 7\).

blocks.x: Start with \(n\), multiply by \(-3\), then add \(2\), and you reach \(10\), so \(-3n + 2 = 10\). The times-\(-3\) is the inner box and the add-\(2\) is the outer box, so peel from the outside in. Subtract \(2\) first, then divide by \(-3\). Watch the signs, because the answer will not be a whole number. Solve \(-3n + 2 = 10\) and type \(n\) as a fraction in lowest terms, including its sign.
hints: The outer box is the \(+2\), since the \(2\) was added last. Strip it off first by subtracting \(2\) from both sides, and see what is left on each side.

After subtracting, you have \(-3n = 8\). The inner box is times \(-3\), so undo it by dividing both sides by \(-3\). A positive divided by a negative is negative, and \(8\) and \(3\) share no common factor, so it stays as a fraction.
blocks.sol: Subtract \(2\) from both sides to get \(-3n = 8\), then divide both sides by \(-3\). $$\frac{-3n}{-3} = \frac{8}{-3}$$ A positive over a negative is negative, and \(8\) and \(3\) share no common factor, so \(n = \boxed{-8/3}\). Checking, \(-3 \cdot \left(-\tfrac{8}{3}\right) = 8\) and \(8 + 2 = 10\). A negative fraction is a perfectly good solution.

blocks.x: Peel from the outside in. To free a variable, undo the operations wrapped around it in reverse order, the last thing done first, like taking off your coat before your shirt. A constant added on the outside comes off before the number multiplying on the inside, and each peel is the opposite operation done to both sides at once, so the scale stays balanced and the answer never moves. When the variable finally stands alone, plug your number back in to be sure both sides agree.

blocks.cap: Undo from the outside in. \(4x-9=7\) was built by \(\times 4\) then \(-9\), so peel the last layer first, add 9 to get \(4x=16\), then divide by 4 to get \(x=4\). Check that \(4\cdot4-9=7\).

blocks.x: Real equations are not always neat. Sometimes the variable's side holds several terms, like \(2x + 3x\), or a group that still needs distributing, like \(4(t - 7)\). Tidy that side first, using the like-terms and distributing work from 6.1, before you peel off a single layer. In every equation here the variable stays on one side and the other side is a plain number.

A delivery rider's day reads \(5k + 2 + 3k - 7 = 19\), where \(k\) is the number of trips. Do not undo anything yet. First tidy the cluttered left side by combining like terms, exactly as in 6.1, then isolate \(k\). Solve \(5k + 2 + 3k - 7 = 19\) and type the value of \(k\).
hints: Resist undoing anything first. The left side is a pile of like terms, so combine them before you touch the right side. Add up the \(k\) terms, \(5k\) and \(3k\), and separately add up the plain numbers, \(2\) and \(-7\).
After combining you get \(8k - 5 = 19\), a clean two-step. Add \(5\) to both sides to get \(8k = 24\), then divide both sides by \(8\).
blocks.sol: Combine like terms on the left. The \(k\) terms give \(5k + 3k = 8k\), and the plain numbers give \(2 - 7 = -5\). $$8k - 5 = 19$$ Add \(5\) to both sides for \(8k = 24\), then divide both sides by \(8\). The rider made \(\boxed{3}\) trips. Tidying first turns a four-term pile into a plain two-step equation, so there is less to keep track of.

blocks.x: A side can hide its real shape inside a group. In \(6(2 - q) = 30\), the outer times-\(6\) has to reach both pieces inside before anything else can happen, so it meets the \(2\) and the \(-q\), and that minus sign rides along. Distribute carefully, then peel the two-step equation. Solve \(6(2 - q) = 30\) and type the value of \(q\).
hints: Hand the outer \(6\) to both pieces inside the group before you do anything else. The \(6\) hits the \(2\) and it also hits the \(-q\), so watch that the sign rides along. The left side turns into \(12 - 6q\).
Now you have \(12 - 6q = 30\), a plain two-step. Subtract \(12\) from both sides to get \(-6q = 18\), then divide both sides by \(-6\). A positive divided by a negative is negative.
blocks.sol: Distribute the \(6\) across the group. $$6(2 - q) = 30$$ $$12 - 6q = 30$$ Subtract \(12\) from both sides to get \(-6q = 18\), then divide both sides by \(-6\). $$q = \frac{18}{-6} = \boxed{-3}$$ Checking, \(2 - (-3) = 5\) and \(6 \times 5 = 30\). The minus sign rides along when you distribute, so \(-q\) becomes \(-6q\), not \(6q\).

blocks.x: A paint mixer uses two thirds of a tank to fill today's order, so \(\frac{2}{3}x = 10\), where \(x\) is the tank's capacity in liters. The variable is wrapped in a multiply-by-\(\frac{2}{3}\) box, so multiply both sides by the reciprocal \(\frac{3}{2}\), which turns the \(\frac{2}{3}\) into a plain \(1\). Solve \(\frac{2}{3}x = 10\) and type the value of \(x\).
hints: The variable is being multiplied by \(\frac{2}{3}\). To undo a multiplication you do the opposite. Multiplying both sides by the reciprocal \(\frac{3}{2}\) will flip the \(\frac{2}{3}\) back to \(1\) and leave \(x\) alone on the left.
Multiply both sides by \(\frac{3}{2}\). The left side becomes \(x\). The right side becomes \(10 \cdot \frac{3}{2}\), so work out \(\frac{30}{2}\).
blocks.sol: Multiply both sides by the reciprocal \(\frac{3}{2}\). $$\frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{3}x = \frac{3}{2} \cdot 10$$ On the left, \(\frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{3} = 1\), leaving \(x\). On the right, \(10 \cdot \frac{3}{2} = \frac{30}{2} = 15\), so the tank holds \(\boxed{15}\) liters. Multiplying both sides by \(3\) and then dividing by \(2\) gets you the same place, since that is the same two moves.

blocks.cap: The bar under \(x+4\) means the whole group is split into \(5\) equal slices, so the equation reads \(\frac{x+4}{5}=3\). Multiplying both sides by that denominator \(5\) hands the five slices back as one whole group and undoes the division, turning the equation into the clean \(x+4=15\), since \(3\times 5=15\). From there it is one more step, peel off the \(+4\) from both sides, and the variable stands alone at \(x=11\).

blocks.x: Tidy before you peel. Clean up the side holding the variable before you touch both sides. Distribute any group with a number out front and gather every like term, until that side is one variable term and one plain number. If the variable sits under a fraction bar, the denominator is the outermost layer, so clear it first by multiplying both sides by it and the fraction disappears. A fractional coefficient like \(\frac{2}{3}x = 8\) comes off the same way, by multiplying both sides by the flipped fraction. All of this is fair both-sides work, so the answer never moves, and once that side is as short as it goes you start peeling.

Solving for the variable is often just the first half of a question. A ticket booth's group passes \(x\) satisfy \(5(x - 2) = 35\), but the manager wants the wristband count, given by \(2x + 1\). First solve \(5(x - 2) = 35\) for \(x\), then compute \(2x + 1\). Type that final number.
hints: Start by solving for \(x\) on its own. The whole left side is multiplied by \(5\), so undo that first by dividing both sides by \(5\). Set the value of \(x\) aside, because the question is really asking about \(2x+1\).
Dividing both sides by \(5\) gives \(x-2=7\), so adding \(2\) to both sides gives \(x=9\). Now substitute into the wristband rule. Work out \(2\times 9+1\) and type that single number.
blocks.sol: Divide both sides by \(5\) to get \(x - 2 = 7\), then add \(2\) to both sides for \(x = 9\). The question wants the wristband count, so substitute into \(2x + 1\). $$2(9) + 1 = 18 + 1 = 19$$ The booth hands out \(\boxed{19}\) wristbands. Solving for the variable was only half the job, so reread what the question actually asks for before typing an answer.

blocks.x: Sometimes you are handed the variable and must hunt for a missing number. A game designer's win happens when a score \(x\) satisfies \(3x + c = 20\), where \(c\) is a fixed bonus she still has to choose. She wants \(x = 4\) to count as a win, which means \(x = 4\) must be a solution. Substitute \(4\) for \(x\), then solve for \(c\). Type the value of \(c\).
hints: You know what \(x\) is this time, so put it to work. A solution is a value that makes the equation true, so replace \(x\) with \(4\) in \(3x + c = 20\) and see what the equation turns into.
After substituting you get \(12 + c = 20\). Now \(c\) is the only unknown left, sitting on one side. Undo the \(+12\) by subtracting \(12\) from both sides.
blocks.sol: Substitute \(4\) in for \(x\), since \(x = 4\) has to make the equation true. $$3(4) + c = 20$$ $$12 + c = 20$$ Subtract \(12\) from both sides. $$c = \boxed{8}$$ Checking, \(3(4) + 8 = 12 + 8 = 20\). Nothing new is going on here. The letter you solve for is just whichever one is still unknown.

blocks.x: A community garden shares a total across \(4\) equal plots, ending with \(6\) beds each, so \(\dfrac{3(m-2)+2m}{4} = 6\), where \(m\) is beds per row. Peel the outermost box first by multiplying both sides by \(4\), then distribute, combine like terms, and isolate \(m\). Solve \(\dfrac{3(m-2)+2m}{4} = 6\) and type the value of \(m\).
hints: The whole left side is wrapped in a division by 4. That is the outermost box, so undo it first. Multiply both sides by 4 to clear the denominator, and the equation becomes \(3(m-2)+2m=24\).

Now distribute the 3 across \(m-2\) to get \(3m-6\), then add the \(2m\). The like terms \(3m\) and \(2m\) combine into \(5m\), so the left collapses to \(5m-6=24\). Add 6 to both sides, then divide both sides by 5.
blocks.sol: Multiply both sides by \(4\) to clear the denominator. $$3(m-2)+2m=24$$ Distribute the \(3\), then combine the like terms \(3m\) and \(2m\). $$3m-6+2m=24$$ $$5m-6=24$$ Add \(6\) to both sides for \(5m=30\), then divide both sides by \(5\). $$m=\boxed{6}$$ The denominator was the outermost layer, so it had to come off before there was anything to tidy inside. Checking, \(3(4)+12=24\) and \(24 \div 4 = 6\).

review.x: A diver's instrument reads higher as she rises, and her start reading \(x\) satisfies \(x + 12 = 5\), where negative values mean below the surface. Solve \(x + 12 = 5\) and type the value of \(x\).
hints: The variable \(x\) is being added to by \(12\). To undo adding \(12\), do the opposite to both sides and subtract \(12\).
After you subtract \(12\) from the right side, you are computing \(5 - 12\), which lands below zero.
review.sol: Subtract \(12\) from both sides. $$x + 12 = 5$$ $$x + 12 - 12 = 5 - 12$$ $$x = \boxed{-7}$$ Checking, \(-7 + 12 = 5\), which matches the right side. Landing below zero is fine, it just means she started below the surface.

review.x: A jar holds some marbles, and after \(6\) more are dropped in it holds \(20\). With \(n\) the starting count, that is \(n + 6 = 20\). Solve for \(n\) and type the value.
hints: The \(6\) is being added to \(n\), so undo it by subtracting \(6\) from both sides at once.
Subtracting \(6\) from the left leaves \(n\) all by itself, and subtracting \(6\) from the right turns \(20\) into \(20 - 6\).
review.sol: Subtract \(6\) from both sides. $$n + 6 - 6 = 20 - 6$$ $$n = 14$$ The jar started with \(\boxed{14}\) marbles. Checking, \(14 + 6 = 20\).

review.x: Four identical packs together hold \(9\) mini sets, so \(4m = 9\), where \(m\) is how many fit in one pack. Solve for \(m\) and type the value as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Right now \(m\) is multiplied by 4. To get \(m\) by itself, do the opposite of multiplying and divide both sides by 4.
Dividing both sides by 4 gives \(m = \tfrac{9}{4}\). Check that 9 and 4 share no common factor, so it is already in lowest terms.
review.sol: Divide both sides by 4, which gives \(m = \tfrac{9}{4}\). Since 9 and 4 share no common factor, that is already in lowest terms, so \(\boxed{9/4}\). Checking, \(4 \cdot \tfrac{9}{4} = 9\).

review.x: A descending drone's tracker satisfies \(-6y = 54\). Divide both sides by \(-6\) to solve. Type the value of \(y\), including its sign.
hints: The \(y\) is being multiplied by \(-6\), so to get \(y\) by itself, divide both sides of the equation by \(-6\).
Work out the right side. You need \(54\) divided by \(-6\), which is \(-9\).
review.sol: Divide both sides by \(-6\). That leaves \(y\) on the left, and on the right \(54\) divided by \(6\) is \(9\), while a positive divided by a negative is negative. So \(y = \boxed{-9}\). Checking, \(-6 \times (-9) = 54\), which matches the right side.

review.x: A vending machine charges \(x\) per snack plus a flat \(\$7\) fee, and \(3\) snacks come to \(\$22\), so \(3x + 7 = 22\). Peel the constant, then the coefficient. Solve and type the value of \(x\).
hints: The \(7\) is just added on at the end, so peel it off first. Subtract \(7\) from both sides to get \(3x\) by itself.
Now you have \(3x = 15\). Since \(3x\) means \(3\) times \(x\), divide both sides by \(3\) to find \(x\).
review.sol: Subtract \(7\) from both sides. $$3x + 7 - 7 = 22 - 7$$ $$3x = 15$$ Then divide both sides by \(3\). $$x = \boxed{5}$$ Checking, \(3(5) + 7 = 15 + 7 = 22\). The constant comes off before the coefficient, because adding the \(7\) was the last thing done.

review.x: A baker uses \(w\) cups on each of two trays and sets aside \(3\), using \(4\) cups in all, so \(2w - 3 = 4\). Add \(3\) to both sides, then divide by \(2\). Type \(w\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The lone number on the left is the \(-3\). Move it out of the way first by adding 3 to both sides, so the \(2w\) stands alone.
After adding 3 you get \(2w = 7\). Now undo the times-2 by dividing both sides by 2.
review.sol: Add 3 to both sides to get \(2w = 7\), then divide both sides by 2. Each tray takes \(\boxed{7/2}\) cups. Checking, \(2 \cdot \frac{7}{2} = 7\) and \(7 - 3 = 4\), which matches the right side.

review.x: Tidy the busy left side first, then hunt for the value. Solve \(7t - 2 - 4t + 5 = 18\) and type the value of \(t\).
hints: The left side has two \(t\) terms and two plain numbers. Combine them first. The \(t\) terms give \(7t - 4t = 3t\), and the numbers give \(-2 + 5 = 3\), so the equation becomes \(3t + 3 = 18\).
Now peel away the outside layers. Subtract \(3\) from both sides to undo the \(+3\), then divide both sides by \(3\) to undo the multiplication.
review.sol: Combine like terms on the left. The \(t\) terms give \(7t - 4t = 3t\), and the numbers give \(-2 + 5 = 3\). $$3t + 3 = 18$$ Subtract \(3\) from both sides for \(3t = 15\), then divide both sides by \(3\). $$t = \boxed{5}$$ Checking, \(7 \cdot 5 - 2 - 4 \cdot 5 + 5 = 35 - 2 - 20 + 5 = 18\).

review.x: Five identical kits each ship with \(4\) items missing, so each holds \(d - 4\), and all five total \(15\), giving \(5(d - 4) = 15\). Distribute the \(5\) first, then isolate \(d\). Type the value of \(d\).
hints: Distribute the 5 across the parentheses. \(5(d-4)\) becomes \(5d-20\), so the equation reads \(5d-20=15\).
Now the variable is alone on the left as one term. Undo the \(-20\) by adding 20 to both sides, then undo the times 5 by dividing both sides by 5.
review.sol: Distribute the 5 across the parentheses. $$5(d-4)=15$$ $$5d-20=15$$ Add 20 to both sides for \(5d = 35\), then divide both sides by 5. $$d=\boxed{7}$$ Checking, each kit holds \(7 - 4 = 3\) items, and five kits hold \(5 \cdot 3 = 15\).

review.x: A triangle has three equal edges, each measuring \(2k + 5\), and its perimeter is \(9\), so \(3(2k + 5) = 9\). Distribute, then solve. Type the value of \(k\).
hints: Multiply the \(3\) through the parentheses first. \(3 \cdot 2k\) and \(3 \cdot 5\) give you \(6k+15=9\).
Now the variable is alone on the left once you peel away the constant. Subtract \(15\) from both sides, then divide both sides by \(6\).
review.sol: Distribute the \(3\) across the group. $$3(2k+5)=9$$ $$6k+15=9$$ Subtract \(15\) from both sides for \(6k = -6\), then divide both sides by \(6\). $$k=\boxed{-1}$$ Checking, each edge is \(2(-1)+5=3\), and three edges of \(3\) give a perimeter of \(9\).

review.x: Three fifths of a tank's capacity \(x\) comes to \(9\) liters, so \(\frac{3}{5}x = 9\). Multiply both sides by the reciprocal \(\frac{5}{3}\) to free \(x\). Type the value of \(x\).
hints: The variable is being multiplied by \(\frac{3}{5}\). To undo that, multiply both sides by the reciprocal, which is \(\frac{5}{3}\).
Compute \(9 \cdot \frac{5}{3}\). The \(9\) and the \(3\) share a factor, so this lands on a clean whole number.
review.sol: Multiply both sides by the reciprocal \(\frac{5}{3}\). $$\frac{5}{3} \cdot \frac{3}{5}x = \frac{5}{3} \cdot 9$$ The two fractions cancel to \(1\) on the left, and on the right \(\frac{5}{3} \cdot 9 = \frac{45}{3} = 15\), so \(x = \boxed{15}\). Checking, \(\frac{3}{5} \cdot 15 = \frac{45}{5} = 9\).

review.x: A fractional coefficient scales \(b\), and the other side is negative, so \(\tfrac{2}{7}b = -4\). Free \(b\) by multiplying both sides by the flipped fraction \(\tfrac{7}{2}\), carrying the negative through. Type the value of \(b\).
hints: The coefficient \(\tfrac{2}{7}\) is multiplying \(b\), so undo it by multiplying both sides by its reciprocal \(\tfrac{7}{2}\). On the left, \(\tfrac{7}{2}\cdot\tfrac{2}{7} = 1\), which leaves a bare \(b\). On the right you still have to work out \(\tfrac{7}{2}\cdot(-4)\), and a positive times a negative stays negative.
Multiplying the right side, \(\tfrac{7}{2}\cdot(-4) = \tfrac{7\cdot(-4)}{2} = \tfrac{-28}{2} = -14\). So the whole equation collapses to \(b = -14\). Keep that minus sign, it does not disappear.
review.sol: Multiply both sides by the reciprocal \(\tfrac{7}{2}\). $$\tfrac{7}{2}\cdot\tfrac{2}{7}b = \tfrac{7}{2}\cdot(-4)$$ The left side collapses to \(b\), and the right side is \(\tfrac{-28}{2}\), so \(b = \boxed{-14}\). Checking, \(\tfrac{2}{7}\cdot(-14) = \tfrac{-28}{7} = -4\). The minus sign carries straight through the multiplication.

review.x: A value \(3h + 2\) shared equally among \(4\) display cases gives \(5\) each, so \(\dfrac{3h+2}{4} = 5\). Undo the division first by multiplying both sides by \(4\), then solve. Type the value of \(h\).
hints: The left side is one big quantity divided by \(4\). Multiply both sides by \(4\) to clear the denominator, which turns the equation into \(3h+2=20\).
Now you have \(3h+2=20\). Peel the layers in reverse. Subtract \(2\) from both sides, then divide both sides by \(3\).
review.sol: Multiply both sides by \(4\) to clear the denominator. $$3h+2=20$$ Subtract \(2\) from both sides for \(3h = 18\), then divide both sides by \(3\). $$h=\boxed{6}$$ Checking, \(3 \cdot 6 + 2 = 20\) and \(\frac{20}{4} = 5\). The denominator is the outermost layer, so it comes off before anything on the top.

review.x: A quantity \(5x + 2\) divided into \(4\) equal parts gives \(6\) each, so \(\frac{5x+2}{4} = 6\). Clear the denominator first by multiplying both sides by \(4\), then solve. Type \(x\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The variable is trapped over a denominator of \(4\). Undo that division first by multiplying both sides by \(4\), which turns the left side into just \(5x+2\).
Once you have \(5x+2=24\), subtract \(2\) from both sides to get \(5x=22\), then divide both sides by \(5\). Since \(22\) is not a multiple of \(5\), your answer stays a fraction.
review.sol: Multiply both sides by \(4\) to clear the denominator. $$5x+2 = 24$$ Subtract \(2\) from both sides for \(5x = 22\), then divide both sides by \(5\). $$x = \boxed{22/5}$$ Since \(22\) and \(5\) share no common factor, that is already in lowest terms. Checking, \(5 \cdot \frac{22}{5} + 2 = 24\) and \(\frac{24}{4} = 6\).

review.x: You are told \(n = 5\) is a solution of \(2n + c = 17\), so plugging in \(5\) must make it true. Substitute \(n = 5\), then solve for the constant \(c\). Type the value of \(c\).
hints: Replace \(n\) with 5 everywhere it shows up. The equation becomes \(2(5) + c = 17\), and \(2(5)\) is just 10.
Now you have \(10 + c = 17\). Ask what number added to 10 lands on 17, or subtract 10 from both sides.
review.sol: Substitute 5 in for \(n\), since \(n = 5\) has to make the equation true. $$2(5) + c = 17$$ $$10 + c = 17$$ Subtract 10 from both sides. $$c = \boxed{7}$$ Checking, \(2(5) + 7 = 10 + 7 = 17\), which matches the right side.

blocks.x: In 6.2 the unknown sat on one side and the plain numbers on the other. Real situations are not always so tidy, and the same unknown can show up on both sides at once. Picture two scooter apps, one costing \(2m + 5\) and the other \(3m\). They cost the same when \(2m + 5 = 3m\), which has \(m\) on both pans. You cannot isolate the variable while copies sit on each side, so the one new move is to subtract a variable term from both sides until the unknown is on one side only. Everything after that is the same work you did in 6.2.

A locker rental costs \(7x + 2\) and a bike rental costs \(4x + 17\), each over the same number of days \(x\), and today they came out equal, so \(7x + 2 = 4x + 17\). The new idea is that the balance rule lets you take the same term off both pans, and that term can be a variable. Subtract \(4x\) from both sides to clear the \(x\) off the right, then solve the one-sided equation. Solve \(7x + 2 = 4x + 17\) and type the value of \(x\).
hints: Both sides carry an \(x\) term. Subtract the smaller one, \(4x\), from each side so the variable survives on only one side.
After subtracting \(4x\) you get \(3x + 2 = 17\). Now it is an ordinary two-step equation, subtract 2 then divide by 3.
blocks.sol: Subtract \(4x\) from both sides. On the left \(7x - 4x = 3x\), and the right loses its \(x\) term, leaving \(3x + 2 = 17\). Subtract 2 to get \(3x = 15\), then divide by 3 for \(x = 5\). Both sides come out to 37, so \(\boxed{5}\). Taking the same variable term off both pans is legal for the same reason taking off the same number is, the scale stays level.

blocks.x: Gather the variable to one side. When the unknown shows up on both sides, the one new move is to collect every variable term onto a single side. The balance principle still applies, so adding or subtracting the same variable term on both sides keeps the equation true, exactly as it did with plain numbers. Once the variable sits on only one side, you are back to the one-sided equations from 6.2 and you finish the same way.

blocks.cap: \(4x=x+6\) has an \(x\) on each pan. Lifting one \(x\) off both at once keeps the scale level and clears the variable from the right, leaving \(3x=6\), and one division gives \(x=2\).

blocks.x: When the bigger pile of variables is on the right, a little planning avoids negatives. In \(9 + 3x = 7x + 1\), subtracting \(7x\) would leave a negative \(x\) term, so instead subtract the smaller variable term, \(3x\), from both sides so the survivor stays positive. Solve \(9 + 3x = 7x + 1\) and type the value of \(x\).
hints: Compare the two variable terms, \(3x\) and \(7x\). Subtract the smaller, \(3x\), from both sides to keep the remaining \(x\) term positive.
After subtracting \(3x\) you get \(9 = 4x + 1\). Subtract 1, then divide by 4.
blocks.sol: The variable terms are \(3x\) and \(7x\). Subtract the smaller, \(3x\), from both sides so the survivor stays positive. The left becomes \(9\) and the right becomes \(4x + 1\), giving \(9 = 4x + 1\). Subtract 1 from both sides to get \(8 = 4x\), then divide by 4 to get \(x = 2\). A quick check, the original left is \(9 + 3(2) = 15\) and the right is \(7(2) + 1 = 15\), so \(\boxed{2}\).

blocks.x: Before moving anything across, tidy each side on its own. The left side of \(5x + 4 - 2x = x + 12\) has like terms hiding in it, so combine them first, then gather the variable onto one side. Solve \(5x + 4 - 2x = x + 12\) and type the value of \(x\).
hints: The left side is not in simplest form. Combine \(5x\) and \(-2x\) into \(3x\), so the equation reads \(3x + 4 = x + 12\).
Now subtract \(x\) from both sides to get \(2x + 4 = 12\), then finish with the usual two steps.
blocks.sol: Combine the like terms on the left, \(5x - 2x = 3x\), so the equation is \(3x + 4 = x + 12\). Subtract \(x\) from both sides to get \(2x + 4 = 12\), subtract 4 to get \(2x = 8\), then divide by 2 for \(x = 4\). Both sides come out to 16, so \(\boxed{4}\). Tidying each side on its own first keeps the gathering step from getting messy.

blocks.x: A group can hide the variable until you distribute. In \(2(3x - 4) = 4x + 6\), expand the left side with the distributive property from 6.1, then collect the variable on one side. Solve \(2(3x - 4) = 4x + 6\) and type the value of \(x\).
hints: Distribute the 2 across the group first. \(2(3x - 4)\) becomes \(6x - 8\), so the equation is \(6x - 8 = 4x + 6\).
Subtract \(4x\) from both sides to get \(2x - 8 = 6\), then add 8 and divide by 2.
blocks.sol: Distribute the 2 on the left, \(2(3x - 4) = 6x - 8\), so the equation becomes \(6x - 8 = 4x + 6\). Gather the variable by subtracting \(4x\) from both sides, leaving \(2x - 8 = 6\). Add 8 to both sides to get \(2x = 14\), then divide by 2 to get \(x = 7\). Check, the left is \(2(3 \cdot 7 - 4) = 2(17) = 34\) and the right is \(4(7) + 6 = 34\), so \(\boxed{7}\).

blocks.x: The full recipe. First simplify each side on its own by distributing and combining like terms. Next gather all the variable terms onto one side and the plain numbers onto the other, moving the smaller variable term so the survivor stays positive. Then isolate the variable the way you did in 6.2, and finish by checking your answer in the original equation. Every linear equation in this course comes apart this way.
About 1,700 years ago Diophantus of Alexandria used shorthand symbols for unknowns. He discarded any puzzle whose answer came out negative, calling such results absurd.

Nothing says the meeting value has to be a whole number. Solve \(8x - 3 = 3x + 4\), gathering the variable onto one side, and let the answer be a fraction if that is where it lands. Type \(x\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Subtract \(3x\) from both sides to get \(5x - 3 = 4\).
Add 3 to get \(5x = 7\), then divide both sides by 5. The answer is a fraction, so leave it in lowest terms.
blocks.sol: Subtract \(3x\) from both sides to get \(5x - 3 = 4\). Add 3 to get \(5x = 7\), then divide by 5 for \(x = \tfrac{7}{5}\), which is already lowest terms since 7 and 5 share no common factor. Both sides come out to \(\tfrac{41}{5}\), so \(\boxed{7/5}\). A fraction answer is an ordinary result here, nothing needs rounding or fixing.

blocks.x: When a fraction sits in the equation, clear it first. In \(\dfrac{x}{3} + 4 = x - 2\), multiply every term on both sides by \(3\) to wipe out the denominator, then solve the both-sides equation that remains. Solve \(\dfrac{x}{3} + 4 = x - 2\) and type the value of \(x\).
hints: Multiply every term on both sides by 3 to clear the denominator. \(\tfrac{x}{3}\) becomes \(x\), the 4 becomes 12, and the right side \(x - 2\) becomes \(3x - 6\).
Now solve \(x + 12 = 3x - 6\). Subtract \(x\), then finish.
blocks.sol: Clear the fraction by multiplying every term on both sides by 3. The left \(\tfrac{x}{3} + 4\) becomes \(x + 12\), and the right \(x - 2\) becomes \(3x - 6\), so the equation is \(x + 12 = 3x - 6\). Subtract \(x\) from both sides to get \(12 = 2x - 6\), add 6 to get \(18 = 2x\), then divide by 2 to get \(x = 9\). Check in the original, the left is \(\tfrac{9}{3} + 4 = 3 + 4 = 7\) and the right is \(9 - 2 = 7\), so \(\boxed{9}\).

blocks.x: Try to solve \(6x + 5 = 6x - 2\). Gather the variable terms by subtracting \(6x\) from both sides and watch what remains. How many solutions does this equation have? Type the single number.
hints: Subtract \(6x\) from both sides and watch the variable disappear entirely.
You are left with \(5 = -2\), which is never true. An equation that reduces to a false statement has no solution, so the count is 0.
blocks.sol: Gather the variable by subtracting \(6x\) from both sides. Every \(x\) vanishes, and you are left with \(5 = -2\). That statement is false, and no value of \(x\) can ever make \(6x + 5\) equal \(6x - 2\), since the two sides always differ by 7. So the equation has no solution, a count of \(\boxed{0}\).

blocks.x: Now try \(3(2x + 4) = 6x + 12\). Distribute the left side, gather the variable, and notice what is left. To feel the result, test three values, \(x = 0\), \(x = 7\), and \(x = 20\). How many of those three are solutions? Type the single count.
hints: Distribute the 3 on the left. \(3(2x + 4)\) becomes \(6x + 12\), which is exactly the right side.
Since both sides are identical, every value of \(x\) is a solution, so all three test values work. Count them.
blocks.sol: Distribute the left side, \(3(2x + 4) = 6x + 12\), which is precisely the right side. Gathering the variable by subtracting \(6x\) leaves \(12 = 12\), a statement that is always true. That means every value of \(x\) is a solution, so the equation has infinitely many. In particular all three test values \(x = 0\), \(x = 7\), and \(x = 20\) work, which is \(\boxed{3}\) of the three. The equation is really just two ways of writing the same expression, the equivalent expressions you met in 6.1.

blocks.x: Special cases. Once in a while the variable terms cancel completely when you gather them, leaving a statement with no variable at all. If that statement is true, like \(6 = 6\), then every number was a solution, so there are infinitely many. If it is false, like \(5 = -2\), then no number can ever work, so there is no solution. The leftover statement tells you which case you are in.

A shop compares two presses over \(t\) hours. The old press prints \(3(2t + 5)\) pages and the new one prints \(4t + 27\), and at one hour count they match. Distribute the left side, gather the variable, and find it. Solve \(3(2t + 5) = 4t + 27\) and type the value of \(t\).
hints: Distribute the 3 first. \(3(2t + 5)\) becomes \(6t + 15\), so the equation is \(6t + 15 = 4t + 27\).
Subtract \(4t\) from both sides to get \(2t + 15 = 27\), then subtract 15 and divide by 2.
blocks.sol: Distribute the left side, \(3(2t + 5) = 6t + 15\), so the equation is \(6t + 15 = 4t + 27\). Gather the variable by subtracting \(4t\) from both sides, leaving \(2t + 15 = 27\). Subtract 15 to get \(2t = 12\), then divide by 2 to get \(t = 6\). Check, the old press gives \(3(2 \cdot 6 + 5) = 3(17) = 51\) and the new gives \(4(6) + 27 = 51\), so \(\boxed{6}\).

review.x: Solve \(9x = 5x + 12\) and type the value of \(x\).
hints: Subtract \(5x\) from both sides to gather the variable on the left.
That leaves \(4x = 12\). Divide both sides by 4.
review.sol: Subtract \(5x\) from both sides, \(9x - 5x = 4x\), leaving \(4x = 12\). Divide both sides by 4 to get \(x = 3\). Check, the left is \(9(3) = 27\) and the right is \(5(3) + 12 = 27\), so \(\boxed{3}\).

review.x: Solve \(7y + 4 = 2y + 24\) and type the value of \(y\).
hints: Subtract \(2y\) from both sides to get \(5y + 4 = 24\).
Subtract 4, then divide by 5.
review.sol: Subtract \(2y\) from both sides to get \(5y + 4 = 24\). Subtract 4 to get \(5y = 20\), then divide by 5 to get \(y = 4\). Check, the left is \(7(4) + 4 = 32\) and the right is \(2(4) + 24 = 32\), so \(\boxed{4}\).

review.x: First combine like terms on the left, then gather the variable. Solve \(7t + 2 - 3t = t + 17\) and type the value of \(t\).
hints: Combine \(7t\) and \(-3t\) into \(4t\), so the equation reads \(4t + 2 = t + 17\).
Subtract \(t\) from both sides to get \(3t + 2 = 17\), then finish.
review.sol: Combine the like terms on the left, \(7t - 3t = 4t\), so the equation is \(4t + 2 = t + 17\). Subtract \(t\) from both sides to get \(3t + 2 = 17\), subtract 2 to get \(3t = 15\), then divide by 3 to get \(t = 5\). Check, the left is \(7(5) + 2 - 3(5) = 22\) and the right is \(5 + 17 = 22\), so \(\boxed{5}\).

review.x: Distribute the left side first, then gather the variable. Solve \(6(w - 2) = 3w + 6\) and type the value of \(w\).
hints: Distribute the 6. \(6(w - 2)\) becomes \(6w - 12\), so the equation is \(6w - 12 = 3w + 6\).
Subtract \(3w\) from both sides to get \(3w - 12 = 6\), then add 12 and divide by 3.
review.sol: Distribute the left side, \(6(w - 2) = 6w - 12\), so the equation is \(6w - 12 = 3w + 6\). Subtract \(3w\) from both sides to get \(3w - 12 = 6\). Add 12 to get \(3w = 18\), then divide by 3 to get \(w = 6\). Check, the left is \(6(6 - 2) = 24\) and the right is \(3(6) + 6 = 24\), so \(\boxed{6}\).

review.x: Solve \(7x + 1 = 2x + 9\) and type \(x\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Subtract \(2x\) from both sides to get \(5x + 1 = 9\).
Subtract 1 to get \(5x = 8\), then divide by 5. The answer is a fraction in lowest terms.
review.sol: Subtract \(2x\) from both sides to get \(5x + 1 = 9\). Subtract 1 to get \(5x = 8\), then divide by 5 to get \(x = \tfrac{8}{5}\). Since 8 and 5 share no common factor, it is in lowest terms. Check, the left is \(7 \cdot \tfrac{8}{5} + 1 = \tfrac{56}{5} + \tfrac{5}{5} = \tfrac{61}{5}\) and the right is \(2 \cdot \tfrac{8}{5} + 9 = \tfrac{16}{5} + \tfrac{45}{5} = \tfrac{61}{5}\), so \(\boxed{8/5}\).

review.x: Clear the denominator first by multiplying every term by \(2\). Solve \(\dfrac{y}{2} + 5 = y - 1\) and type the value of \(y\).
hints: Multiply every term on both sides by 2. \(\tfrac{y}{2}\) becomes \(y\), the 5 becomes 10, and the right side \(y - 1\) becomes \(2y - 2\).
Now solve \(y + 10 = 2y - 2\). Subtract \(y\), then finish.
review.sol: Multiply every term on both sides by 2 to clear the fraction. The left \(\tfrac{y}{2} + 5\) becomes \(y + 10\), and the right \(y - 1\) becomes \(2y - 2\), so the equation is \(y + 10 = 2y - 2\). Subtract \(y\) from both sides to get \(10 = y - 2\), then add 2 to get \(y = 12\). Check, the left is \(\tfrac{12}{2} + 5 = 6 + 5 = 11\) and the right is \(12 - 1 = 11\), so \(\boxed{12}\).

review.x: Gather the variable in \(3x - 4 = 3x + 5\) by subtracting \(3x\) from both sides, then read what remains. How many solutions does it have? Type the single number.
hints: Subtract \(3x\) from both sides and watch the variable vanish.
You are left with \(-4 = 5\), which is never true, so there is no solution. The count is 0.
review.sol: Subtract \(3x\) from both sides. The variable cancels completely and leaves \(-4 = 5\), a false statement. The two sides always differ by 9, so no value of \(x\) can ever make them equal. The equation has no solution, a count of \(\boxed{0}\).

review.x: Distribute the left side of \(4(x + 2) = 4x + 8\) and compare it with the right. Test \(x = 1\), \(x = 9\), and \(x = 50\). How many of the three are solutions? Type the count.
hints: Distribute the 4. \(4(x + 2)\) becomes \(4x + 8\), exactly the right side.
The two sides are identical, so every value of \(x\) works, including all three test values. Count them.
review.sol: Distribute the left side, \(4(x + 2) = 4x + 8\), which matches the right side exactly. Gathering the variable leaves \(8 = 8\), always true, so every value of \(x\) is a solution and there are infinitely many. All three test values \(x = 1\), \(x = 9\), and \(x = 50\) work, which is \(\boxed{3}\) of the three.

review.x: Two gyms charge by the month. Over \(m\) months gym A costs \(7m + 18\) and gym B costs \(9m\). Find the month count where they cost the same. Solve \(7m + 18 = 9m\) and type the value of \(m\).
hints: Subtract \(7m\) from both sides to get \(18 = 2m\).
Divide both sides by 2.
review.sol: Subtract \(7m\) from both sides to gather the variable on the right, leaving \(18 = 2m\). Divide both sides by 2 to get \(m = 9\). Check, gym A costs \(7(9) + 18 = 81\) and gym B costs \(9(9) = 81\), so they match at \(\boxed{9}\) months.

blocks.x: A word problem is one fact written twice, once in plain English and once in algebra, and the two versions say the identical thing. A sentence like a number tripled and then reduced by four gives eleven is just \(3x - 4 = 11\) put into words. The same five steps handle every one of them. Read the whole problem, name the unknown with a letter, translate each phrase by its meaning, solve, then answer the exact question asked and check it against the original story.

An arcade prize machine doubles the bronze tokens you feed it and drops in \(7\) bonus tokens, and after Priya's turn the screen reads \(31\). In other words, seven more than twice her tokens is thirty-one. How many bronze tokens did Priya feed the machine?
hints: Give the unknown a name first. Let \(x\) be the number of tokens Priya fed the machine. Now translate the sentence one phrase at a time. What does "twice her tokens" become, and what does "seven more than" that become? The words "is thirty-one" hand you the equals sign.

Twice her tokens is \(2x\), and seven more than that is \(2x + 7\). The phrase "is thirty-one" sets it equal to \(31\), so your equation is \(2x + 7 = 31\). Subtract \(7\) from both sides, then divide by \(2\).
blocks.sol: Let \(x\) be the tokens Priya fed in. Twice her tokens plus seven is thirty-one, so \(2x + 7 = 31\). Subtract \(7\) to get \(2x = 24\), then divide by \(2\), so she fed in \(\boxed{12}\) tokens. Translate one phrase at a time. Twice gives \(2x\), seven more than adds \(7\), and is hands you the equals sign.

blocks.x: A beekeeper scoops out exactly a third of whatever a jar holds, pours it into a bottle, then stirs in \(9\) more ounces. The bottle then weighs \(17\) ounces, since here the word of means multiply. How many ounces of honey did the jar hold at the start?
hints: Let \(x\) stand for the number of ounces the jar held at the start. Now read the words one piece at a time and turn each piece into math. "A third of the amount" becomes \(\tfrac{1}{3}x\), "increased by nine" adds \(9\), and "is seventeen" gives you the equals sign and the \(17\).
Your equation is \(\tfrac{1}{3}x + 9 = 17\). Subtract \(9\) from both sides to get \(\tfrac{1}{3}x = 8\), then multiply both sides by \(3\) to undo the one third.
blocks.sol: Let \(x\) be the ounces the jar held at the start. A third of that plus nine ounces is seventeen, so \(\tfrac{1}{3}x + 9 = 17\). Subtract \(9\) to get \(\tfrac{1}{3}x = 8\), then multiply both sides by \(3\), so the jar held \(\boxed{24}\) ounces. Check it. A third of \(24\) is \(8\), and nine more is \(17\).

blocks.x: Maya tapes streamers to a wall, and the number on the wall is nineteen fewer than the number in her box, which counts out to \(40\). Watch the order. Fewer than subtracts from the number, so this is \(x - 19\), not \(19 - x\). How many streamers were in Maya's box to start with?
hints: Let \(x\) be the number of streamers in the box. The phrase "nineteen fewer than the number" means you start with the number and take 19 away, so it becomes \(x - 19\), not \(19 - x\). Set that equal to 40.
Solve \(x - 19 = 40\) by adding 19 to both sides. Then read your answer back into the words to make sure nineteen fewer really lands on forty.
blocks.sol: Let \(x\) be the streamers in Maya's box. Nineteen fewer than that number is \(x - 19\), and it equals forty, so \(x - 19 = 40\). Add \(19\) to both sides, so the box held \(\boxed{59}\) streamers. Fewer than reverses the order you hear it in. Reading it as \(19 - x\) would give \(-40\) streamers.
